historical_timeline.summary: Born in Spilsby, Lincolnshire, the ninth of twelve children of a merchant.
Enters the Royal Navy at 14; fights at Copenhagen and Trafalgar and is left with a mild hearing loss.
Slightly wounded at the battle of Lake Borgne.
First overland Arctic expedition: starvation, eleven men dead; known as the man who ate his boots.
Marries Eleanor Anne Porden; she dies of tuberculosis in 1825, a year after their daughter's birth.
Second overland expedition; knighted in 1829; marries Jane Griffin in 1828.
Arrives in Van Diemen's Land as Lieutenant-Governor; recalled under censure, back in England by June 1844.
Seeks the command of the Northwest Passage expedition; senior officials question his age, build and tolerance of cold.
A severe bout of influenza, not fully recovered when the ships sail.
Erebus and Terror sail from the Thames with 129 men; beset off King William Island from September 1846.
Dies during the expedition; the cause and place are not recorded.
The ships are abandoned; no man survives the retreat. Later studies of the crew's remains find lead, tuberculosis and signs of hardship; the causes are disputed.
The wrecks of Erebus and Terror are found with the help of Inuit knowledge.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Fitness assessment of an older man before a multi-year Arctic expedition, with high blood pressure and obesity found at the pre-expedition medical: a 58-year-old naval officer chosen to command an expedition that will be years beyond the reach of hospital care. The episode covers confirming the diagnosis with home readings and treating stage 2 hypertension under the 1844 AHA/ACC guideline, choosing a medicine that needs no laboratory monitoring and suits dehydration and cold; cardiovascular risk with ECG, lipids, HbA1c, kidney function, urine albumin, echocardiography and an exercise treadmill test, and the PREVENT and Pooled Cohort risk estimates; weight managed by his own goals and without stigma; vitamin C and vitamin D and nutrition planning for years without fresh food; food safety, with canned-food quality, lead and botulism as modern risks; cold injury and hypothermia prevention under the Wilderness Medical Society guidelines; vaccinations, including rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis; dental care before departure; noise-induced hearing loss; mental health in isolation and polar darkness; a medical kit and an evacuation plan; and influenza in the weeks before departure, with oseltamivir and decongestant avoidance.

assessment.assessment: No barrier found so far. Age alone does not exclude him; what matters is his heart, his blood pressure and his capacity for hard work in the cold. Because he will be beyond rescue, the bar for testing is lower than for ordinary life: an echocardiogram for stage 2 hypertension and a symptom-limited exercise treadmill test, done once he is free of any acute illness, are advised before final clearance. Weight is one factor among many and is his to set goals for; it is not a reason to refuse him the command

Stage 2 hypertension confirmed at home, with no target-organ damage so far; a urine albumin is still needed. Treatment with medicine is indicated, with a goal below 130/80. Amlodipine is the best fit for his circumstances: it needs no blood tests, keeps for years in blister packs, and does not cause the low sodium, low potassium or kidney injury that a diuretic or a renin-angiotensin blocker can cause with the dehydration and cold diuresis of polar work. Ankle swelling is its main side effect. A home monitor with a spare cuff and written dose rules for the ship's surgeons should go with him

Vitamin C stores last only weeks to a few months without intake, and the vitamin C in stored juice and food loses strength over time, so a daily vitamin C tablet stored sealed, cool and dark is advised for the whole expedition, with the stores checked and scurvy signs taught. His vitamin D is insufficient in midwinter and polar darkness will lower it further: vitamin D3 daily is advised. Rations should be energy-dense, because work in the cold can need far more calories than at home. Lead-soldered food cans have long been abandoned in the United States, but imported or old cans should be checked; his baseline blood lead is normal. Botulism is rare but cannot be treated at sea: bulging, leaking, dented or spurting cans should be discarded unopened, no home-canned food carried, and the early signs (double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, descending weakness) taught to the surgeons

Prevention is the main tool: layered clothing with vapor control, dry socks and mitts, enough food and fluid, no alcohol or tobacco before exposure, and buddy checks of faces, hands and feet. Frostbitten tissue should be rewarmed in warm water only when it can be kept from refreezing, without rubbing; hypothermia should be recognized early, with insulation, shelter and gentle handling of the cold, confused or stiff man. Amlodipine does not raise the risk of cold injury

Bring tetanus up to date and give the vaccines due at his age (PCV20, recombinant zoster, hepatitis B), and give rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis, because Arctic foxes carry rabies and rabies immune globulin will be out of reach. A dental examination before departure is essential: dental pain is among the commonest emergencies on long expeditions. Baseline mood and anxiety are normal; long isolation and months of darkness call for a daily routine of work, light, exercise and sleep, peer support among the officers, and watchfulness for low mood. There is no evacuation for months at a time, so the plan must be a kit, written instructions and his own written wishes for serious illness on board
